title: The International Space Station
summary: Countries that once raced each other teamed up to build the biggest thing ever put in space: the International Space Station. It is as long as a football field, zooms around the whole Earth every hour and a half, and people have lived on it every single day for more than 25 years. Up there, astronauts sleep on the walls, drink recycled water, grow lettuce and do science you cannot do on Earth.

sections.heading: From Rivals to Partners
paragraphs: Imagine trying to build a house where every room is made in a different country, nobody can test whether the rooms fit together until they meet, and the building site is flying around the planet at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. That is roughly what it took to build the International Space Station, or ISS.

In the 1980s the United States planned a big station of its own called Freedom, with help from Europe, Japan and Canada. Meanwhile Russia was running Mir and had decades of experience living in orbit. After the Cold War ended in 1991, it made sense to join forces. Russia brought its long-stay knowledge, its reliable Soyuz spacecraft and its Progress cargo ships; the Americans brought the Space Shuttle and a huge budget; Europe, Japan and Canada brought laboratories, robots and skilled astronauts. The Shuttle–Mir flights of the 1990s, described in the last part, were a kind of rehearsal.

The deal was written down in an international treaty called the Intergovernmental Agreement, signed on 29 January 1998. Five space agencies run the station together: NASA for the United States, Roscosmos for Russia, the European Space Agency (ESA), which speaks for many European countries, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). Altogether about 15 countries are partners. Each partner owns and runs its own pieces, and they share out crew time, electricity and supplies by agreement. It is a bit like a block of flats where every family owns its own apartment but everyone shares the lift, the water and the heating.

Building began on 20 November 1998, when a Russian Proton rocket launched the first module from Baikonur in Kazakhstan. It was called Zarya, meaning 'sunrise'. Zarya was built in Russia but paid for by the United States, and in the early days it supplied electricity, steering and storage. Just two weeks later, on 4 December 1998, the Space Shuttle Endeavour carried up Unity, an American connecting module called a node. Using the Shuttle's robotic arm, the crew grabbed Zarya and joined the two together. On 7 December, astronauts Jerry Ross and James Newman made the station's first spacewalk to connect power and data cables between them. Those two modules, one Russian and one American, bolted together in orbit, were the first seed of the station.

In July 2000 the Russian service module Zvezda, meaning 'star', arrived. It contained living quarters, toilets, life-support machines and engines to keep the station in its orbit. Now people could move in.

Over the next eleven years dozens of pieces followed. The American laboratory Destiny arrived in February 2001. Europe's laboratory Columbus, built in Italy and Germany, came in February 2008. Japan's laboratory Kibo, the largest single module on the station, arrived in stages in 2008 and 2009; it has a small 'porch' outside where experiments can sit directly in space. Long metal beams called trusses, carrying gigantic solar panels and radiators, were added piece by piece. In 2010 a dome-shaped window module called the Cupola was installed, with seven windows that give astronauts the best view of Earth ever built into a spacecraft. Building the station took more than 40 launches, including 36 Space Shuttle assembly flights, plus well over a hundred spacewalks. The newest Russian modules, the Nauka laboratory and the Prichal docking hub, arrived in 2021. Nobody knows the exact total cost, but it is often estimated at well over 100 billion US dollars, making the ISS one of the most expensive objects humans have ever built.

sections.heading: Never Empty Since 2000
paragraphs: On 31 October 2000 a Soyuz rocket lifted off from Baikonur carrying three men: the American commander Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. You might remember Krikalev as the cosmonaut who was aboard Mir when the Soviet Union broke apart. On 2 November 2000 they docked, opened the hatch and floated in. They were Expedition 1, the first crew to live on the International Space Station.

Here is a remarkable thing. Since that day, there has never been a moment when the station was empty. Crew after crew has arrived and handed over to the next, with no gap at all. That means that since 2 November 2000, there have always been humans living in space. If you are reading this and you were born after that date, you have never lived a single second when every human being was on the ground. Somebody was always up there, sleeping, working or looking down at your town.

Each crew stays for an 'expedition', usually about six months, and the expeditions are numbered. By the mid-2020s the numbers had passed 70. Some astronauts have stayed much longer. In 2015 and 2016 the American Scott Kelly and the Russian Mikhail Kornienko spent nearly a year aboard, about 340 days. In 2022 and 2023 the American Frank Rubio stayed 371 days, the longest single flight by an American, after his planned six months were extended when his Soyuz spacecraft sprang a coolant leak and a replacement had to be sent. The record for the longest single stay ever still belongs to Valeri Polyakov, from his 437 days on Mir.

Today the station usually has a crew of about seven. Many different spacecraft take people and supplies up and down. The Russian Soyuz has carried crews since the very beginning. After the Space Shuttle retired in 2011, Soyuz was for nine years the only way for anyone to reach the station, and American astronauts bought seats on it. Robot cargo ships also visit: Russia's Progress, and over the years Europe's Automated Transfer Vehicle, Japan's HTV, nicknamed Kounotori or 'white stork', and American commercial ships. The story of the private companies whose spacecraft now fly crews from Florida comes later in this Deep Dive.

Hundreds of people from about 26 countries have visited the ISS. They include scientists, doctors, engineers, pilots and a few paying private visitors. Some countries sent their first astronauts there, such as Hazzaa AlMansouri of the United Arab Emirates in 2019. In June 2025 Shubhanshu Shukla, an Indian Air Force pilot flying on a private Axiom mission, became the first Indian to visit the station, and only the second Indian ever to fly in space, 41 years after Rakesh Sharma.

sections.heading: A Football Field Flying Around the World
paragraphs: The ISS is huge. From one end to the other it measures about 109 metres, almost exactly the length of an American football field including the end zones, and much longer than the giant Airbus A380 airliner. Most of that width is the main truss, a long backbone of metal beams holding eight enormous solar wings. The station weighs about 420 tonnes, about as much as 300 cars. Its pressurised modules, the parts where people can live and breathe without spacesuits, have about as much space inside as a six-bedroom house, or the inside of a Boeing 747 jumbo jet.

Those solar panels produce up to about 75 to 90 kilowatts of electricity, enough to run dozens of homes. Since 2021, new rolled-out solar arrays have been added on top of the old ones to boost the power as the original panels wear out. Big white panels called radiators get rid of extra heat into space, because in a vacuum there is no air to carry heat away, so a spacecraft has to shed it as invisible infrared light.

The station orbits about 400 kilometres above the ground, roughly the distance from London to Paris, but straight up. It travels at about 7.7 kilometres every second, around 28,000 kilometres per hour. That is fast enough to cross the whole of the United States in about ten minutes. It goes once around the Earth about every 90 minutes, which means astronauts see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours. If they looked out of the Cupola at every one, they would never get any sleep.

Remember from Part 10 that the station is not floating in 'no gravity'. At 400 kilometres up, Earth's gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. The station and everyone inside it are falling around the Earth together, endlessly, missing the ground because they are moving sideways so fast. That is why the astronauts float.

The station is not perfectly safe from the air, either. Even at 400 kilometres there is a tiny trace of atmosphere, which slowly drags on the station and makes it sink a little lower every day. Every so often, engines on Zvezda or on a docked cargo ship fire to push it back up. The station can also dodge: if a piece of space junk is predicted to pass too close, controllers fire the engines to shift it out of the way. Its walls are lined with special shields, made of layers of metal and fabric spaced apart, that can shatter small specks before they reach the living areas.

You can see the ISS yourself without a telescope. On many clear nights, shortly after sunset or before sunrise, it appears as a very bright, steady star sliding silently across the sky in a few minutes, brighter than any real star. It shines because sunlight reflects off its solar panels while the ground below is already dark. NASA's 'Spot the Station' website and many phone apps tell you exactly when it will pass over where you live. It is a strange and wonderful feeling to wave at it and know that people are waving back, even if they cannot see you.

sections.heading: A Day in the Life, Upside Down
paragraphs: What is it actually like to live up there? The station runs on Greenwich Mean Time, the time zone of London, as a compromise between the control centres in Houston, Moscow, Germany, Japan and Canada. A typical weekday starts at about six in the morning, when the crew wakes up, washes, has breakfast and joins a planning call with the ground. Then they work through a detailed timeline of experiments, repairs and exercise, set by mission controllers, until the evening. Weekends are lighter, with time for cleaning, calling family and looking out of the window.

Sleeping is easy in one way: you never need a mattress. Each astronaut has a tiny private cabin about the size of a phone box, with a sleeping bag fastened to the wall, a laptop, a reading light and a few family photographs. Because there is no up or down, it does not matter whether the bag is on a wall, the floor or the ceiling. Astronauts zip themselves in loosely so they do not drift around and bump into things in the night, and some say their arms float up in front of them like a sleepwalker's while they doze. Fans must blow air through every cabin, because in weightlessness warm air does not rise. Without a breeze, the carbon dioxide you breathe out would collect in a bubble around your face.

Food comes from Earth, packed in pouches and cans. Some is dried and needs hot water squirted in; some is heated in a small food warmer; some, like nuts and biscuits, is eaten just as it is. Crews from different countries often swap treats: Russian soups, Japanese curry, European cheeses. Bread is a problem because crumbs float away and can get into equipment or people's eyes, so astronauts eat tortillas instead. Salt and pepper come as liquids, the salt dissolved in water and the pepper in oil, so the grains do not drift around. Fresh fruit arrives on cargo ships and disappears quickly. Many astronauts say food tastes blander in space, probably because fluids shift towards the head and make it feel like having a blocked nose.

Then there is the toilet, the question every child asks. Without gravity, nothing falls downwards, so space toilets use moving air instead, like a gentle vacuum cleaner. Each astronaut has a personal funnel attached to a hose for urine, and a small seat for solid waste, which is sucked into bags and packed into containers that are later loaded into a cargo ship and burned up in the atmosphere. Astronauts train carefully on Earth to use it, with a camera mock-up to check their aim.

The urine does not go to waste. Water is heavy and expensive to launch, so the station's Water Recovery System collects urine, sweat and even the moisture breathed into the air, filters it, boils it and cleans it into drinking water. Astronauts like to joke that 'yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee'. For years the system recycled more than 90 percent of the water, and in 2023 NASA announced that new equipment had pushed it to about 98 percent. That kind of recycling will be essential on a trip to Mars, where there will be no resupply ships.

There are no showers. Astronauts wash with wet towels and special no-rinse soap and shampoo, and squeeze water onto their skin, where it clings as a wobbly layer. Brushing teeth means swallowing the toothpaste or spitting it into a towel. Haircuts are done with clippers attached to a vacuum hose, so the hair does not float away. Even crying is different: tears do not roll down your cheeks but collect in a blob around your eyes.

Oxygen to breathe comes mostly from splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity, and machines scrub carbon dioxide out of the air. Fire is one of the biggest dangers on any spacecraft, so the crew practises emergency drills, and every module has extinguishers and masks.

sections.heading: Staying Strong Without Gravity
paragraphs: On Earth, every step you take, every stair you climb and even just standing up works your bones and muscles against gravity. In orbit, that load disappears. The body is clever and lazy at the same time: if a bone or muscle is not being used, it slowly gets rid of it. Before modern exercise machines, astronauts on long missions lost about 1 to 2 percent of the mineral in some of their bones, such as the hips and spine, every month. Their leg and back muscles shrank too, and their hearts got a little weaker because pumping blood around a weightless body is easier.

That is why ISS astronauts exercise for about two hours every day. They have three main machines. The first is a treadmill. To stop themselves floating off it, runners wear a harness attached to elastic bungee cords that pull them down onto the moving belt. The second is an exercise bike called CEVIS, which has no seat: astronauts clip their shoes into the pedals and hold the handlebars. The third and most important is the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device, or ARED. Since there is no gravity to make weights heavy, ARED uses vacuum cylinders, like giant syringes, to create a pulling force of up to a few hundred kilograms. Astronauts can do squats, deadlifts and other weightlifting exercises on it just as they would in a gym.

It works. Since ARED arrived in 2008, crews coming home after six months have kept much more of their bone strength and muscle than earlier space travellers. Some even return with stronger arms than before. Even so, when astronauts land after a long stay, they often feel dizzy and heavy at first and need days or weeks of physical therapy to walk normally again. Some say even holding up their own head feels like hard work for the first day.

Weightlessness changes the body in other ways too. Fluids that gravity normally pulls into your legs float upwards, so astronauts get puffy faces and thin legs, which they call 'puffy face, bird legs'. Their spines stretch out a little, so most astronauts grow by a few centimetres in space and shrink back on Earth. Some develop changes in the shape of their eyes that can blur their vision, a problem doctors are still studying. The inner ear, which senses balance, gets confused at first, and many new astronauts feel a bit sick for their first few days.

One famous experiment used identical twins. In 2015 and 2016 Scott Kelly spent nearly a year aboard the ISS, while his identical twin brother Mark, also an astronaut, stayed on the ground. Because they share the same genes, scientists could compare them to see which changes were caused by space. They found changes in how some of Scott's genes were switched on and off, in his immune system and in his eyes. Most of the changes went back to normal within months of his return, which was encouraging news for anyone planning a long trip to Mars.

Space is also stressful for the mind. Astronauts live in a small space with the same few people for months, far from family, with a busy schedule. To help, they have regular video calls home, private talks with doctors and psychologists, films, music, books and care packages of favourite foods. Many say that looking down at Earth, with its thin glowing blue atmosphere and no borders visible from above, is the best medicine of all. Some astronauts describe a deep change of feeling called the 'overview effect': a sense of how fragile and precious our planet is.

sections.heading: A Laboratory Like No Other
paragraphs: The main reason the ISS exists is science. It is a laboratory where gravity is almost switched off, something you cannot do on Earth for more than a few seconds at a time. Over its lifetime, thousands of experiments from more than 100 countries and areas have been run aboard, many of them designed by school students.

Plants are one favourite subject. In a small growth chamber called Veggie, lit by pink and blue LED lights, astronauts have grown lettuce, cabbage, kale and even flowers such as zinnias. On 10 August 2015 the crew ate the first lettuce grown on the American side of the station, a red romaine variety, after cleaning it with sanitising wipes. Later crews grew chili peppers and radishes. Learning how plants find their way without gravity, using light and water instead, helps scientists plan for growing food on long missions, and helps farmers on Earth too.

Fire and fluids behave in fascinating ways in orbit. A candle flame in space is not tall and pointed but round and blue, because hot air does not rise. Experiments discovered so-called cool flames, which burn at much lower temperatures than normal flames and can keep going for minutes in microgravity. Water forms floating spheres that wobble like jelly. Studying these things helps engineers design better engines, fire safety and medical devices.

Medicine benefits as well. Protein crystals, the tiny regular structures scientists use to work out the shape of molecules, often grow larger and more perfect in weightlessness, which helps researchers design new medicines. Studies of astronauts' bones have helped doctors understand osteoporosis, a disease that makes elderly people's bones fragile. In 2016 the astronaut Kate Rubins became the first person to read the DNA of living things in space, using a pocket-sized sequencer, showing that crews could one day identify germs aboard without sending samples home.

Physicists have used the station to do very strange things. In 2018 an instrument called the Cold Atom Lab cooled a cloud of atoms to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, and made a Bose–Einstein condensate, sometimes called the fifth state of matter, in orbit for the first time. Outside, a big detector called the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer has recorded more than 100 billion cosmic-ray particles since 2011, hunting for clues about dark matter. Cameras and sensors on the outside watch Earth's forests, storms, fires and lightning.

Much of the work outside the station is done by robots. The most famous is Canadarm2, Canada's robotic arm, installed in April 2001. It is about 17.6 metres long when fully stretched, with joints like a shoulder, elbow and wrist, and it can move objects weighing up to about 116 tonnes, including whole spacecraft, because in orbit nothing is heavy, although large things still need to be moved slowly and carefully. Canadarm2 has a clever trick: it has a grabbing 'hand' at both ends, so it can let go with one end and grab a new fixture with the other, flipping end over end along the station like an inchworm. Astronauts operating it from inside use it to catch visiting cargo ships out of the sky and berth them to the station, to move spacewalking astronauts around like a cherry-picker crane, and to install new equipment. In 2008 it was joined by Dextre, a two-armed robot 'hand' that can do delicate jobs such as changing batteries, so that astronauts do not have to go outside as often.

sections.heading: New Stations, New Nations
paragraphs: The ISS is not the only story in orbit. On 15 October 2003 a Long March 2F rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in the Gobi Desert carrying Yang Liwei, a former fighter pilot, aboard the spacecraft Shenzhou 5. He circled Earth 14 times in about 21 hours before landing safely in Inner Mongolia. China became only the third country, after the Soviet Union and the United States, to launch a person into space on its own rocket. Chinese astronauts are often called taikonauts, from the Chinese word for space.

China then built up its skills step by step. In 2008 a Chinese astronaut made the country's first spacewalk. Two small test laboratories, Tiangong-1 in 2011 and Tiangong-2 in 2016, let crews practise docking and living in orbit; in 2012 Liu Yang became the first Chinese woman in space. Then, on 29 April 2021, a Long March 5B rocket launched Tianhe, meaning 'harmony of the heavens', the core module of a permanent station called Tiangong, which means 'heavenly palace'. Two laboratory modules, Wentian and Mengtian, joined it in 2022, completing the T-shaped station. Tiangong weighs about 100 tonnes, roughly a quarter of the ISS, and orbits at a similar height. Crews of three now live aboard in rotation, and in 2021 Wang Yaping became the first Chinese woman to walk in space.

India is building its own human spaceflight program, called Gaganyaan, which means 'sky vehicle'. Its plan is to launch Indian astronauts on an Indian rocket from Sriharikota, starting with uncrewed test flights, and Indian scientists have also talked about building an Indian space station in the future. Like all future spaceflight plans, the dates may change. The training of Indian astronauts got a boost when Shubhanshu Shukla flew to the ISS in 2025.

Many other countries now send astronauts or build parts of spacecraft. Europe's astronauts have commanded the ISS; Japan's astronauts have lived aboard many times; the United Arab Emirates sent Sultan AlNeyadi for a six-month stay in 2023, and he became the first Arab astronaut to make a spacewalk. Private companies are designing commercial space stations of their own, which they hope will one day rent out space to scientists, companies and visitors.

The ISS will not last forever. Its oldest modules have been in space for more than 25 years, and metal parts slowly wear out, crack and leak. The partners currently plan to keep using it until about 2030. After that, NASA plans to use a special spacecraft, the US Deorbit Vehicle, to push the station down into a remote part of the Pacific Ocean, the same area where Mir ended its life. As with every plan in spaceflight, the exact dates may change. By then, it is hoped, new stations will be ready to take over, so that the chain of humans living in space does not have to be broken.

The ISS may be the greatest example of cooperation in human history: former enemies sharing air, water and meals in a fragile tin can far above the Earth, year after year. But astronauts aboard it never go further than about 400 kilometres from home. Meanwhile, machines without any people inside were travelling millions and even billions of kilometres, to the hot clouds of Venus, the dusty red plains of Mars and beyond the edge of the solar system. It is time to follow the robots.

deepDive: How do you keep about 420 tonnes of hardware, built by five agencies over more than a decade, working in orbit for over 25 years? Engineers point to three big ideas. The first is modularity. Every module was designed to fit inside the Shuttle's payload bay or on top of a Proton or other rocket, so no piece is much wider than about 4.5 metres. Standard connecting ports, power and data plugs, and robot-friendly grapple fixtures meant pieces made in Russia, the United States, Italy, Germany, Japan and Canada could be joined in orbit without ever having been assembled together on Earth. The second is redundancy: the station has two partly independent segments, Russian and American, each with its own life support, so if one oxygen generator or carbon dioxide scrubber fails, the crew can rely on another. The third is maintainability. Thousands of parts are designed as 'orbital replacement units' that astronauts or Dextre can swap out. Running the station is not cheap. NASA spends roughly 3 to 4 billion US dollars a year on ISS operations, and the total cost to all partners is usually estimated at well over 100 billion dollars, though numbers vary because each country counts differently. Critics argue that the same money could have funded many robotic missions or telescopes, and debates about the station's scientific value have continued since the 1990s. Supporters reply that it has taught us how to keep humans healthy for a year in space, that results such as better water recycling and bone-loss treatments matter on Earth, and that the partnership itself kept Russia and the West cooperating even through difficult political times. The station also faces ageing problems: since 2019 a slow air leak in a small tunnel in the Russian segment has needed repeated patching. The orbit itself has a famous number, 51.6 degrees. That is the angle between the station's path and the equator, chosen so that Soyuz rockets launched from Baikonur in Kazakhstan can reach it. It also means the ISS passes over places where about 90 percent of the world's population lives.
funFact: Because the ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes, astronauts aboard see roughly 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day.
